title: Why You Stay Logged In: Sessions Cookies Explained ⚡
ig_caption:
How computer networks & routing work under the hood: DNS → HTTPS → sessions cookies
What actually happens after you login—zero mystery, just verified tickets

• sessions & cookies: your “login state” rides on a signed token
• login once: server sets a session cookie (over HTTPS)
• ticket checks 0 passwords: requests carry a cookie back to the server
• hash match: server validates the token/session hash (e.g., 3f9a… ✓)
• why it stays: routing + sockets deliver the request; auth happens at the app layer

Practical takeaway: In interviews, describe the flow as “client stores a cookie; server verifies it per request”—not “the network remembers you.”

Hot debate: Should long-lived sessions be default, or should rotating session IDs be the safer standard?

fb_caption:
Most people say “cookies keep you logged in,” but that’s only the top layer. Under the hood, your auth experience is the coordination of networking fundamentals (routing/DNS/transport) and application-layer verification (sessions).

Here’s the production-grade mental model:

1) Network path (routing & DNS) isn’t authentication
- Your browser resolves the host (DNS), establishes a route, then opens transport connections (TCP) and sends HTTP requests.
- DNS lookup and routing affect delivery latency/reachability, not whether you’re authenticated.

2) Transport delivers; the app decides
- When you login, the server issues a session cookie (signed/tokenized) over HTTPS.
- After that, every request includes the cookie. The network just transports it; your backend validates it.

3) Sessions & cookies: “ticket checks” are the real gate
- The server reads the cookie, computes/compares the expected value (often a hash/signature).
- If the server sees a match (e.g., 3f9a… ✓), it resumes your session without re-asking for credentials.

Trade-offs you should understand:
- Security vs usability: longer session lifetimes reduce friction but increase exposure if stolen.
- Stateless vs stateful sessions: JWT-like tokens can reduce server storage, but revocation/rotation becomes a design challenge.
- Cookie flags matter: Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite reduce common attack surfaces.
- Rotation & hashing: rotating session IDs and verifying signatures/hashes lowers replay risk.

Production lesson: always explain login as “client storage + per-request server verification,” and always separate “network routing” from “auth enforcement.”
